assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a new observational window with a cubic-kilometre neutrino detector in Antarctic ice is exactly the instrument-driven discovery I value: the 2013 evidence for a diffuse high-energy astrophysical flux, then the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 source associations, founded neutrino astronomy.
assessment.attribution: Halzen drove the concept and leadership of IceCube, Karle was central to construction and the design/analysis of the detector, and Spiering was a long-standing leader of the collaboration and the early AMANDA/IceCube program. The credited names fit a three-person prize, but a very large collaboration and the AMANDA/Baikal/ANTARES precursors make the exact split a judgment call.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation is now good: the diffuse flux has been seen in several channels, and the Galactic-plane and NGC 1068 results are recent. The core discovery is stable; source identification is still maturing, but timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should rest on the diffuse-flux discovery alone or also on source associations, some of which are only 3-4 sigma.
How to weigh the contribution of earlier pioneers (AMANDA, Baikal, DUMAND) and whether three names can fairly represent a large collaboration.
I am relying on memory for the detailed history of who led which phase.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022) are a landmark measurement, achieved by synchronising mm-wave VLBI across the globe with exacting calibration. They directly test strong-field gravity and show black-hole shadows.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed imaging the shadow, Doeleman led the building of the global array and the EHT collaboration, and Moran contributed decisive VLBI technology and SMA-based groundwork. The EHT collaboration is about 200 people, so any three-person prize leaves out many, and credit allocation is contentious.
assessment.maturity: Two independent targets, multiple years of data and consistent shadow sizes support the result. Interpretation of the ring (emission models, spin) is still developing, but the imaging claim is robust and recognition is timely, as the 2020 prize went to black-hole theory and Genzel/Ghez.
uncertainties: Allocation among Falcke, Doeleman, Moran and other leaders (e.g. the instrument and imaging-algorithm teams).
Whether the prize committee would regard an imaging result as discovery or as confirmation of established general relativity.
Reliance on memory for individual roles.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, via Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reached 1e-18 fractional uncertainty and enable new tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. This is a precision-measurement invention with large and lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori conceived the magic-wavelength lattice clock idea and Ye's group drove it to record accuracy and stability. A two-person prize is clean. Other clock groups (ions, Hall/Hänsch comb prize of 2005) overlap, and I leave the comparison with Hall to my atomic-physics colleagues.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have confirmed the performance and a redefinition of the second is under discussion, so maturity is high. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Atomic physics is outside my own expertise and I defer to colleagues on the relative claims of Katori versus other lattice-clock pioneers.
The overlap with the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and with the 2012 prize for ion control may weigh on novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Precision CMB anisotropy mapping (WMAP and Planck, with predecessor experiments) fixed the cosmological parameters to percent level and established the standard cosmological model. The measurements are among the most consequential in astrophysics.
assessment.attribution: WMAP's leadership of Bennett, the analysis and theory role of Spergel, and the instrument design/experimental contributions of Page form a coherent trio. This omits Planck (Puget and others) and the Mather/Smoot (2006) and Peebles (2019) prizes already cover parts of the field, making fair credit difficult.
assessment.maturity: Results are thoroughly confirmed, and Planck's independent measurements agree; maturity is excellent. Tensions such as H0 do not undermine the core result. Whether the field is saturated after 2006 and 2019 is the issue.
uncertainties: Whether prior CMB prizes already exhaust the topic.
Exclusion of Planck leaders and balloon-based experiments (BOOMERanG, MAXIMA) from the credited set.
Recollection of the specific roles is from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2012 observation of the Higgs boson with ATLAS and CMS at the LHC is a monumental experimental and detector achievement, completing the Standard Model's particle content, and I find the instrument case compelling.
assessment.attribution: The 2013 prize already recognised Englert and Higgs. A prize for the experimental discovery would have to choose among machine builder (Evans), the ATLAS and CMS leaders (Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) and thousands of collaborators; this is the hardest allocation problem on the list. Three names from the five credited is arbitrary to some degree.
assessment.maturity: The discovery has been confirmed with extensive coupling and spin-parity measurements, and the interpretation is stable. The question is timing: the prize committee may regard the 2013 prize as covering it, and it conflicts with a collaboration-centred award model.
uncertainties: Unresolved credit between machine, two experiments and individual leaders.
Statutes limit laureates to three and committee precedent against awards to large collaborations.
Possible view that the 2013 prize already settled the matter.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon pixel and microstrip detectors transformed particle tracking and vertexing, and made modern LHC physics (b-tagging, Higgs, top) possible, with spin-offs into imaging and space instruments. I rate detector-technology prizes highly, following the Charpak precedent.
assessment.attribution: Heijne's hybrid pixel concept at CERN, Parker's microstrip/pixel work and Snoeys' monolithic and readout-chip developments are credited. The field is broad (Kemmer, Hallewell, the Medipix/Timepix and CCD lines) so priority and attribution are not clean.
assessment.maturity: The technology is widely adopted and independently reproduced in all LHC experiments and beyond, so it is mature and stable. A long time has passed since the original inventions, so recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Which of several parallel inventions (CCDs, hybrid pixels, monolithic active pixels) is decisive.
The set may not match the best-supported historical credit; I rely on memory and would ask for expert review.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The SASE X-ray free-electron laser has opened femtosecond, atomic-resolution X-ray science, with LCLS, SACLA and the European XFEL producing new results in chemistry, biology and materials. It is a major accelerator-instrument achievement.
assessment.attribution: Pellegrini's early SASE proposals and FEL theory, Kim's theory and design work and Saldin's group's contributions (with Schneidmiller and Yurkov at DESY) make for a plausible set. Other claimants (Bonifacio, Madey, Huang, Emma) and the operational LCLS team complicate priority.
assessment.maturity: The principle has been demonstrated repeatedly and facilities are operating, so maturity is high. Whether it is a physics discovery or an engineering one is a matter for the committee.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Bonifacio, Madey and the LCLS builders.
Fit with the physics prize criteria for an enabling facility.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with cold atoms in optical lattices (the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, quantum gas microscopes, Hubbard-model simulators) has turned many-body theory into a laboratory-controlled science. The impact is broad and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the Mott transition, and Esslinger extended the work to fermions. Credit with four names must be cut to three, and other leaders (Cirac, Lewenstein, Kasevich, Ketterle) weigh on that. I am outside my expertise here, and defer to colleagues.
assessment.maturity: The core demonstrations are widely reproduced, with quantum gas microscopes by several groups, so confirmation is strong. Quantum simulation advantage claims are still being sharpened.
uncertainties: Whether Esslinger or others should replace one of the three proposed names.
Condensed-matter and atomic-physics relevance is judged outside my area.
